# Psalm 1 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview: Structure and Character

**Spurgeon** calls Psalm 1 “THE PREFACE PSALM … the text upon which the whole of the Psalms make up a divine sermon.” He divides it into two parts: vv.1–3 (the blessedness of the godly) and vv.4–6 (the doom of the ungodly). (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php)

**Don Carson (Reformed/TGC)** identifies it as a “wisdom psalm” — wisdom literature deals in “ideal absolutes” without footnotes, forcing a choice between two ways. He notes the structure: vv.1–3 describe the righteous, vv.4–5 the unrighteous, and v.6 is the final summarizing contrast. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/two-ways-to-live-psalm-1/)

---

## v. 1 — “Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, or set foot on the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of mockers.”

**The word “Blessed.”** The Hebrew *esher* is a plural noun (“blessednesses”), conveying multiplicity and intensity of blessing. Spurgeon reads it as “Oh, the blessednesses!” and notes the Psalm opens with a benediction just as Christ’s Sermon on the Mount does. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php) Guzik adds that *esher* derives from *ashar*, meaning “to be straight” or “to be right” — true happiness comes from being right with God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-1/) Gill notes the Targum renders it “the goodness of the man,” and that the man is “doubly blessed, a thrice happy and blessed man; blessed in things temporal and spiritual.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

**Negative description.** The righteous man is first described by what he does *not* do — three negations. Spurgeon says this negative description is “more absolute and peremptory than affirmatives,” because a positive might leave room for him to do both; the negative “clears him at all times.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php)

**The threefold progression.** Guzik, Spurgeon, Gill, and the Pulpit Commentary all see a descending progression of sin: *walking* (casual listening to ungodly advice), *standing* (habituated participation in sinful behaviour), and *sitting* (settled identification — becoming a teacher and mocker). Spurgeon: “They have taken their degree in vice, and as true Doctors of Damnation they are installed.” Guzik states this progression moves from “thinking, to behaving, to belonging.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-1/)

**Martin Luther** (quoted in Spurgeon/Precept Austin) interprets “counsel” as “decrees and doctrines” — ungodly men rule themselves by their own counsel and present their errors in the garb of prudence. “To stand” depicts obstinacy and stiff-neckedness. “To sit in the seat” means “to teach, to act the instructor,” as the scribes sat in Moses’ seat (Matt 23:2). Luther warns against those who “fill the church with the opinions of philosophers, with the traditions of men, and with the counsels of their own brain, and oppress miserable consciences, setting aside … the word of God.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-1-commentary)

**Adam Clarke** (quoted in Spurgeon/Precept Austin) distinguishes the three characters: the *ungodly* man has his counsel (“live an honest life, make no fuss about religion”); the *sinner* has his particular way of transgressing (his “easily besetting sin”); the *scorner* “has sat down — is utterly confirmed in impiety, and makes a mock at sin.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-1-commentary)

**Christological reading.** Gill notes that some ancient interpreters (Augustine, Jerome) saw the Psalm as describing the “JUST ONE, i.e. the Lord Jesus.” Gill also applies it to Joseph of Arimathea, who did not consent to the counsel against Christ (Luke 23:51). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

**Carson** observes that the psalmist breaks poetic form by giving only one positive criterion in v.2 instead of the expected three positives matching the three negatives — this forces attention onto the one thing that matters. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/two-ways-to-live-psalm-1/)

---

## v. 2 — “But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night.”

**“The law of the LORD.”** Guzik and the Pulpit Commentary agree this means God’s entire revealed word, not only the Mosaic law. Guzik: “Throughout Psalms, the phrase *law of the LORD* is used to describe God’s entire word.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-1/) The Pulpit Commentary says “the Law intended — תורה, not התּורה — is probably not the mere Law of Moses, but God’s law, as made known to man in any way,” though Joshua 1:8 is clearly in view. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/1.htm)

**Gill** identifies it with the evangelical doctrine, the Gospel: “the word here used, signifies ‘doctrine’, and may intend the evangelic doctrine … the same with the law, or doctrine of faith, in Romans 3:27.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

**“Delight.”** Spurgeon: “Man must have some delight, some supreme pleasure. His heart was never meant to be a vacuum.” If a person delights in something, you do not have to beg him to do it. Spurgeon also warns: some may claim “negative purity” (avoiding the ungodly) but lack delight in God’s word — “If not, this blessing belongeth not to you.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php)

**Luther** (quoted by Spurgeon): This delight “does not look at what the law promises, nor at what it threatens, but at this only; that ‘the law is holy, and just, and good.’ … it victoriously bursts its way through poverty, evil report, the cross, death, and hell, and in the midst of adversities, shines the brightest.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-1-commentary)

**“Meditates day and night.”** Guzik contrasts Eastern meditation (emptying the mind — “dangerous, because an empty mind may present an open invitation to deception”) with Christian meditation: filling the mind with God’s word, “carefully thinking about each word and phrase, applying it to one’s self, and praying it back to the Lord.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-1/) Spurgeon quotes Ashwood: “Meditation chews the cud, and gets the sweetness and nutritive virtue of the Word into the heart and life.” Luther describes meditation as “a certain delightful hunting, nay, rather a playing with stags in a forest, where the Lord furnishes us with the stags, and opens to us their secret coverts.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-1-commentary)

**Carson** calls this “the most urgent need of our times … the careful, delighted, repeated, reverent reading, rereading, and meditating upon God’s most Holy Word.” (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-greatest-need-of-our-time-psalm-1/)

---

## v. 3 — “He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither, and who prospers in all he does.”

**“A tree planted.”** Spurgeon emphasises *planted*, not wild: “chosen, considered as property, cultivated and secured from the last terrible uprooting” (cf. Matt 15:13). Gill adds: “not to one that grows of itself, a wild tree … but to one that is removed from its native place and soil, and planted elsewhere,” signifying transplantation into Christ and the church. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

**“By streams of water.”** Spurgeon: “even if one river should fail, he hath another. The rivers of pardon and the rivers of grace, the rivers of the promise and the rivers of communion with Christ, are never-failing sources of supply.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php) The Pulpit Commentary says these are irrigation canals common in Egypt and Babylonia, by which fruit trees were planted — especially date palms needing proximity to water. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/1.htm) Gill sees the rivers as “the river of the love of God … the fulness of grace in Christ … the graces of the Spirit … the word and ordinances of the Gospel.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

**“Fruit in its season.”** Spurgeon: “not unseasonable graces, like untimely figs, which are never full-flavored. But the man who delights in God’s Word … bringeth forth patience in the time of suffering, faith in the day of trial, and holy joy in the hour of prosperity.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php) Guzik notes that fruit takes time and has its season — the righteous should not be discouraged if fruit is not immediately evident. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-1/)

**“Leaf does not wither.”** Spurgeon: “his faintest word shall be everlasting; his little deeds of love shall be had in remembrance. Not simply shall his fruit be preserved, but his leaf also. He shall neither lose his beauty nor his fruitfulness.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php)

**“Whatever he does shall prosper.”** Spurgeon offers an important caution against reading this as a prosperity promise: “We must not always estimate the fulfillment of a promise by our own eye-sight … It is not outward prosperity which the Christian most desires and values; it is soul prosperity which he longs for … Our worst things are often our best things. As there is a curse wrapped up in the wicked man’s mercies, so there is a blessing concealed in the righteous man’s crosses, losses, and sorrows.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php) Guzik similarly says this is not a “Midas Touch” but that “God brings forth something good and wonderful out of everything. Even tough circumstances bring forth something that shall prosper.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-1/)

**Gill** adds: “not so much in things temporal … for in these the good man does not always succeed, but in things spiritual.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

---

## v. 4 — “Not so the wicked! For they are like chaff driven off by the wind.”

**“Not so.”** Spurgeon notes the Vulgate and Septuagint double the negation: “Not so the ungodly, not so” — meaning whatever good is true of the righteous is *not* true of the wicked. “Oh! how terrible is it to have a double negative put upon the promises!” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php) Gill says the repetition is “for the confirmation of the truth of it.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

**“Like chaff.”** Spurgeon calls chaff “intrinsically worthless, dead, unserviceable, without substance, and easily carried away.” The Pulpit Commentary notes chaff is used throughout Scripture “as an emblem of what is weak and worthless” — in ancient winnowing, chaff was thrown into the air until the wind blew it all away. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/1.htm)

**Spurgeon on the doom:** “death shall hurry them with its terrible blast into the fire in which they shall be utterly consumed.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php)

**Gill** expands: the wicked are like chaff “for lightness, vain in their imaginations, light in their principles, frothy in their words, and unstable in all their ways … fit only for everlasting burnings.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

**The contrast of tree vs. chaff.** Guzik: “There is a huge difference between a tree and chaff” — one is rooted, nourished, fruitful, alive; the other is rootless, dry, worthless, dead. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-1/)

---

## v. 5 — “Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.”

**“Not stand in the judgment.”** Spurgeon: “They shall stand there to be judged, but not to be acquitted. Fear shall lay hold upon them there; they shall not stand their ground; they shall flee away; they shall not stand in their own defence; for they shall blush and be covered with eternal contempt.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php)

The **Pulpit Commentary** says “the judgment” (*הַמִּשְׁפָט*) refers to the judgment of the last day, with the Targum, Rashi, and others concurring. The wicked will not be able to “hold up their heads” in that day. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/1.htm)

**Gill** interprets this of both temporal judgment and the last day: “they shall not stand in the same place with the righteous, not at Christ’s right hand, but at his left; they shall not stand with an holy confidence, with intrepidity, and without shame … they will not be acquitted and discharged, but be condemned.” He also addresses the Septuagint/Vulgate rendering “the ungodly shall not rise again in judgment,” rejecting the idea that the wicked are not resurrected — they will rise, but “not to eternal life.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

**“Nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.”** Spurgeon: “All our congregations upon earth are mixed. Every Church hath one devil in it. The tares grow in the same furrows as the wheat … Sinners cannot live in heaven. They would be out of their element. Sooner could a fish live upon a tree than the wicked in Paradise.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php) The Pulpit Commentary adds that sinners will be cast out “not only from heaven, but also from the Church … if not before, at any rate when the ‘congregation’ is finally made up.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/1.htm)

**Guzik** ties this to Daniel 5:27: like Belshazzar, the ungodly are “weighed in the balances, and found wanting” — they have no weight. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-1/)

---

## v. 6 — “For the LORD guards the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.”

**“The LORD knows the way of the righteous.”** Spurgeon renders the Hebrew as “The Lord is knowing the way of the righteous” — a present, continuous knowing. “He is constantly looking on their way, and though it may be often in mist and darkness, yet the Lord knoweth it.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php) The **Pulpit Commentary** explains that God is said to “know” those He approves of and on whom He “lifts up the light of his countenance.” The wicked He does not “know” — He refuses to acknowledge them. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/1.htm) **Gill** likewise: “the Lord approves of and is well pleased with his way of faith and holiness; he knows this person, so as to love him and take delight and pleasure in him.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

The BSB renders this “the LORD guards the way of the righteous,” which **Carson** explains as God “owns it as his. He watches over it. He acknowledges it. He protects it. He nurtures it.” (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/two-ways-to-live-psalm-1/)

**“The way of the wicked will perish.”** Spurgeon: “Not only shall they perish themselves, but their way shall perish too. The righteous carves his name upon the rock, but the wicked writes his remembrance in the sand … he ploughs the sea, and though there may seem to be a shining trail behind his keel, yet the waves shall pass over it.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php) **Carson** says the way of the wicked will be “as significant 50 billion years from now … as tracks on the seashore when the tide is out.” (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/two-ways-to-live-psalm-1/)

**Guzik** closes by noting that Christianity is called “the Way” at least four times in Acts — “Which way are you on?” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-1/)

---

## Distinctive Tradition Readings

### Baptist (Spurgeon)
The notes above are substantially Spurgeon’s. His emphasis falls on: the necessity of delight in Scripture (not mere negative avoidance of evil), the mixed nature of earthly churches (“Every Church hath one devil in it”), soul-prosperity over material prosperity, and eternal separation at the final judgment. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps001.php)

### Reformed Baptist / Particular Baptist (Gill)
Gill reads “the law of the LORD” as the Gospel — “the evangelic doctrine … the law, or doctrine of faith” (Romans 3:27). He stresses God’s sovereignty in “planting” (transplantation from the wild olive into Christ) and the eternal security of the saint (“His leaf also shall not wither … expressive of the saints’ perseverance”). He also explicitly rejects the notion that the wicked are not resurrected — they rise “not to eternal life” but to condemnation. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm)

### Lutheran (Luther)
Luther sees “counsel of the ungodly” as false doctrine — men ruling themselves by their own decrees rather than God’s word, clothing error in the appearance of wisdom. For him, “to sit in the seat” means to teach as an instructor, and the “seat of pestilence” is filled by those who “fill the church with the opinions of philosophers, with the traditions of men.” On meditation, Luther describes it as a “delightful hunting” in the Scriptures, comparing different passages. On delight, he says it loves the law purely because it is “holy, and just, and good,” not for what it promises or threatens. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-1-commentary)

### Reformed / Evangelical (Don Carson, TGC)
Carson emphasises Psalm 1 as Wisdom Literature — it deals in “ideal absolutes,” presenting two ways with no third option. He notes the psalmist breaks the expected poetic symmetry (three negatives matched by three positives) to spotlight the one positive criterion: delight in and meditation on God’s word. This is “the most urgent need of our times.” The final contrast in v.6 is not between persons but between *ways* — “the Lord watches over the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.” (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/two-ways-to-live-psalm-1/)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Guzik, Enduring Word)
Guzik warns that Eastern meditation (emptying the mind) “may present an open invitation to deception or a demonic spirit,” contrasting it with Christian meditation that fills the mind with Scripture. He stresses that the righteous man’s prosperity in v.3 is not a “Midas Touch” guaranteeing wealth — God brings good out of everything, including hardship. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-1/)

---

## Other Views (from accessed material)

**Modern scholarship:** The Pulpit Commentary notes the agricultural background — “rivers of water” refers to irrigation canals common in Egypt and Babylonia where fruit trees (especially date palms) were deliberately planted. It resists attempts to identify a specific tree species, since the psalmist “may not have been thinking of any particular tree.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/1.htm)

**Early Church / Christological:** Gill and Precept Austin note that Augustine, Jerome, and others read Psalm 1 as describing Christ Himself — the one perfectly blessed and righteous Man. This view remained a minority but persistent reading. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/1.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-1-commentary)

**Catholic and Orthodox readings, Methodist/Wesleyan, prosperity gospel, and modern critical scholarship (NET Bible, Bible Odyssey):** These could not be retrieved within the available search and fetch limits for this response.
